items.title: Mobilisation JOJ : Le Président Diomaye Faye imprime une innovation dans sa communication
items.description: À la veille de l’ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026, le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye a choisi de s’adresser aux Sénégalais autrement. Pas de pupitre, pas de décor institutionnel, encore moins de protocole apparent. Un téléphone, une caméra frontale, le drapeau du Sénégal en arrière-plan et un message adressé directement à ses compatriotes. En quelques secondes, le chef de l’État a déplacé le centre de gravité de sa communication. Cette vidéo selfie rompt avec une certaine approche de la parole présidentielle, généralement construite autour de la solennité, de la mise en scène institutionnelle et d’une certaine distance. Ici, le Président parle à hauteur de citoyen, dans un format familier aux usages quotidiens des réseaux sociaux. Son message emprunte à la spontanéité des plateformes numériques, où la proximité compte parfois autant que le contenu. La parole officielle se fait conversationnelle, le cérémonial s’efface au profit d’une adresse directe. Ce choix répond aussi à la nature particulière de l’événement. Les JOJ ne sont pas uniquement une compétition sportive. Ils constituent un rendez-vous de portée internationale dont la réussite dépend également de l’adhésion populaire. En appelant directement les Sénégalais, le Président veut faire de la mobilisation citoyenne une composante à part entière de l’événement. O.BA

items.title: Sahara occidental : à l’ONU, l’Algérie fait le parallèle avec la Palestine
items.description: En utilisant son droit de veto contre la résolution américaine visant à modifier le mandat de la Minurso vendredi 30 octobre, la Russie a sauvé la légalité internationale dans le dossier du Sahara occidental . L'Algérie, par la voix de son représentant à l’ONU, Amar Bendjama, a remercié la Russie pour avoir présenté un projet de reconduite du mandat de la mission ainsi que tous les pays membres qui ont choisi « de ne pas s’associer à une injustice et une atteinte manifeste aux fondements » de l’organisation onusienne. L’Algérie a demandé à participer à la réunion du Conseil en sa qualité de pays voisin, de pays hôte de centaines de milliers de réfugiés sahraouis et d’État membre de l’ONU, « attaché à la légalité internationale et au respect des buts et principes de la Charte des Nations Unies », a expliqué le diplomate algérien dans son intervention dans laquelle il a décortiqué le dossier en six « mots-clés ». Amar Bendjama : « Qui a peur de la démocratie ? » S’adressant aux États-Unis, « pen holder » du dossier, Amar Bendjama a rappelé qu'« être porte-plume est une lourde responsabilité », et « un devoir moral de mériter la confiance des parties, de susciter leur adhésion, par une attitude attentive, impartiale et équitable ». « Ces critères ont-ils été appliqués dans la rédaction du texte qui vous a été soumis aujourd’hui ? Je vous laisse méditer la réponse », a-t-il dit. Évoquant l’autodétermination, qui a « depuis toujours constitué une référence fondamentale pour le règlement du conflit » et qui est « la forme la plus évidente, la plus sûre et la plus incontestable pour le libre exercice par un peuple du choix de son propre avenir », Bendjama s'est demandé « qui a peur de la démocratie » au point de vouloir cantonner l’autodétermination « à l’intérieur d’un statut d’autonomie dont la plupart d’entre vous ne connaissent que le titre, même si vous l’avez cautionné ». La négociation, ce n'est pas « imposer une conclusion prédéterminée » Le représentant de l’Algérie s'est aussi attardé sur l’expression « solution politique mutuellement acceptable ». « La négociation est un cheminement qui demande écoute attentive des protagonistes, patience, et innovation avec pour objectif une solution acceptable par tous, pour tous », a-t-il rappelé. Or, ni les propositions du Front Polisario ni les préoccupations et réserves faites « candidement » par les deux pays voisins, l’Algérie et la Mauritanie n'ont été « entretenues », a-t-il déploré, dénonçant un texte qui considère « ces négociations comme étant achevées, et ce, avant même qu’elles n’aient commencé ». « La négociation doit être un cheminement vers une solution, et non un moyen d’imposer une conclusion prédéterminée », a asséné Bendjama. Quant à la souveraineté, qui est « une des normes contraignantes du droit international », « nul n’a le droit de conférer à une puissance occupante une propriété qu’il ne possède pas de jure », a-t-il soutenu, regrettant l’altération de cette norme qui « ouvre la porte à toutes les aventures, à l’imposition de la volonté du plus fort sur le plus faible ». Un « fait accompli » résultat d’une « transaction indécente » Le cinquième mot-clé du dossier, selon Amar Bendjama, est le « fait-accompli » de l’invasion et l’annexion d’un territoire non autonome que la résolution américaine veut légaliser. « Ce fait accompli est le résultat d’une transaction indécente conclue aux dépens du peuple palestinien, un peuple qui a tant souffert. Et maintenant, c’est au peuple sahraoui que l’on demande de payer de sa propre liberté les dividendes promis comme rétribution à l’occupant », a-t-il dénoncé, en allusion aux accords de normalisation Maroc-Israël en échange de la reconnaissance par les États-Unis de la « souveraineté marocaine » sur le Sahara occidental. « Humanitaire » : triple peine pour les réfugiés sahraouis Évoquant enfin l’« humanitaire », le représentant de l’Algérie à l’ONU a signifié que les réfugiés sahraouis « sont des êtres humains, pas de simples chiffres ». L’initiative, « dont on veut embarquer le HCR », est synonyme d’une « triple peine » pour les réfugiés sahraouis, a mis en garde Bendjama. Il s’agit, a-t-il expliqué, de « la perpétuation de leur souffrance dans le désert du Sahara », d’un « chantage à la famine qui est actuellement en cours, par la réduction drastique des rations alimentaires à une population déjà affectée par un taux alarmant de malnutrition » et d’un « déplacement forcé, proposé comme alternative et solution durable ». En conclusion, Amar Bendjama a assuré que l’Algérie, qui a exercé son droit à l’autodétermination « au prix de lourds sacrifices », continuera « de manière sincère et déterminée à promouvoir une solution juste, durable et mutuellement acceptable qui garantit le droit du peuple sahraoui à l’autodétermination ». L’article Sahara occidental : à l'ONU, l'Algérie fait le parallèle avec la Palestine est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: UK PM 'open' to slavery apology but not reparations
items.description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday he was “open” to the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations. The Labour leader made the remarks days before attending a Commonwealth leaders summit in Antigua and Barbuda, as King Charles III tours the Caribbean. “I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” Burnam wrote in The Guardian newspaper. The transatlantic slave trade was a “brutal and barbaric violation” of the rights of those enslaved, he said, adding that his government wanted a “structured dialogue with those affected”. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.” The king is due to address the Commonwealth summit, which runs from November 1 to 4. Britain’s central role in slavery and the treatment of people in its former colonies has loomed over the 77-year-old monarch’s Caribbean tour. In the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” during the first leg of his visit. The UK has never formally apologised for slavery nor or agreed to pay reparations. Burnham again rejected financial compensation, writing: “I do not believe that is the right answer. “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.” Britain profited for centuries from colonialism and the slave trade. In 1833, parliament passed a law to abolish slavery.

items.title: Guinée : 30 ans avec RFI, 38 avec AFP… Mouctar Bah célébré pour sa carrière exceptionnelle
items.description: Le journaliste Mouctar Bah, correspondant de Radio France Internationale (RFI) en Guinée, a été célébré ce vendredi 30 octobre 2026 à Conakry, à l’occasion de ses 30 années de collaboration avec le média français. La cérémonie a réuni des membres de sa famille, des confrères, des amis et plusieurs personnalités venus lui rendre hommage et saluer un parcours professionnel remarquable, ainsi que ses qualités humaines. Au-delà de ses trois décennies au service de RFI, Mouctar Bah totalise également 38 années de collaboration avec l’Agence France-Presse (AFP). Un parcours jalonné de reportages sur les grands événements qui ont marqué l’histoire politique et sociale de la Guinée. Pour Alpha Abdoulaye Diallo, du journal Le Populaire , le correspondant de RFI constitue une véritable référence pour les jeunes générations de journalistes. « Mouctar Bah incarne cet homme qui inspire toute une génération », a-t-il déclaré. Prenant également la parole, l’ancien journaliste et historien Amadou Diouldé Diallo a mis en avant une qualité qu’il estime particulièrement rare dans le métier : la capacité à concilier notoriété et humilité. « Le problème de Mouctar Bah ne se situe pas au niveau de la compétence. Il se situe dans sa capacité à pouvoir concilier le journaliste célèbre, auréolé de gloire, et l’humilité. C’est cela qui est difficile », a-t-il témoigné. De son côté, l’ancien ministre Lamine Capi Camara a salué la constance et le professionnalisme du journaliste au fil des années. « Trente ans de parole sans avoir une histoire avec qui que ce soit, il faut le faire », a-t-il souligné, en référence à la longévité professionnelle de Mouctar Bah et à sa capacité à préserver ses relations avec les autres. Il a également évoqué ses qualités humaines et sa bonne humeur, tout en rappelant les liens d’amitié qui les unissent. Visiblement ému par cet hommage qu’il affirme ne pas avoir vu venir, Mouctar Bah a exprimé sa gratitude envers les organisateurs et l’ensemble des participants. Il s’est aussi réjoui de cette volonté de célébrer les personnalités de leur vivant, plutôt que d’attendre leur disparition pour reconnaître leurs mérites. « Je ne savais pas que j’étais intéressant, je ne savais pas que j’étais gentil. Je suis très content. Merci à tout le monde pour cette reconnaissance », a-t-il confié, avec émotion et humour. Revenant sur ses nombreuses années de reportage en Guinée, le correspondant de RFI a évoqué plusieurs moments marquants de sa carrière, notamment les élections de 1998, les incursions rebelles aux frontières guinéennes avec le Liberia et la Sierra Leone, ainsi que les grandes mobilisations politiques en faveur de la démocratie et des libertés publiques. Ces événements, au cœur de l’actualité nationale pendant plusieurs décennies, témoignent de la place qu’a occupée Mouctar Bah dans la couverture de l’histoire contemporaine du pays. Après 30 années de collaboration avec RFI et 38 ans avec l’AFP, le journaliste s’impose comme l’un des témoins privilégiés des mutations politiques et sociales de la Guinée. Au-delà de son expérience professionnelle, cet hommage a surtout mis en lumière un parcours marqué par la rigueur, la discrétion et l’humilité, autant de qualités qui lui valent aujourd’hui la reconnaissance de ses pairs.

items.title: Conseil de sécurité : derrière le soutien au texte américain, de profondes réserves sur la position marocaine
items.description: Les déclarations prononcées au Conseil de sécurité vendredi 30 octobre ont révélé des réserves substantielles sur le projet de résolution américain pour le Sahara occidental qui a été bloqué par le véto russe. Plusieurs délégations ont contesté le caractère déséquilibré du texte et dénoncé le risque de prédéterminer l’issue du processus politique. La Russie a estimé que le projet favorisait ouvertement la position marocaine, marginalisait le Front Polisario et écartait les propositions présentées par celui-ci en 2007. Les réserves de la Chine La Chine a également jugé que certaines dispositions imposaient un résultat à l’une des parties, sans consultations suffisamment équilibrées. Plusieurs délégations ont rappelé que le droit à l’autodétermination devait rester au cœur du règlement. Le Pakistan l’a qualifié de droit sacro-saint et inviolable. La Chine a insisté sur la nécessité de consultations équitables garantissant son exercice. La Somalie a estimé que certaines dispositions du projet américain risquaient de préjuger l’issue des négociations. Ces réserves ont conduit ces pays à s’abstenir, malgré des approches parfois différentes du processus politique. Les déclarations de la Lettonie et du Danemark méritent une attention particulière. Bien qu’ils aient voté en faveur du projet américain, les deux pays ont expressément précisé que leur vote ne constituait ni une reconnaissance de la souveraineté marocaine sur le Sahara occidental, ni une approbation de l’autonomie comme résultat prédéterminé. Le Panama a, lui aussi, posé des limites claires à son soutien. Il considère l’autonomie comme une base pour la reprise des négociations, mais il refuse que cette position préjuge de leur résultat. Le Royaume-Uni et la Grèce, tout en soutenant l’approche fondée sur l’autonomie, ont également rappelé que le règlement devait répondre aux exigences de l’autodétermination. Ces positions traduisent une préoccupation commune : la réforme de la MINURSO ne saurait tenir lieu de règlement politique. Ainsi, le soutien au projet américain ne saurait être interprété comme un ralliement général à la position marocaine. Plusieurs délégations ont voté pour le texte tout en refusant explicitement toute reconnaissance de souveraineté ou toute validation anticipée de l’autonomie. Le scrutin a donc mis en évidence une distinction fondamentale entre le soutien à une base de négociation et l’adhésion à l’issue politique que Rabat entend en tirer. La déclaration de l’ambassadeur américain Mike Waltz mérite également d’être relevée. Évoquant les consultations conduites par Washington, il a déclaré : « Nous avons tenu trois séries de discussions à un niveau très élevé, avec les quatre parties, ou plutôt avec les deux parties et les observateurs autour de la table, je vous prie de m'excuser. » « Cette rectification distingue explicitement les deux parties au conflit, le Maroc et le Front Polisario, des deux pays observateurs, l’Algérie et la Mauritanie. Elle contredit ainsi la thèse farfelue défendue par Rabat, qui cherche à présenter l’Algérie comme une partie au conflit Le vote du 30 octobre révèle deux lignes de fracture. Washington veut adapter la mission à une nouvelle dynamique politique et réduire progressivement son rôle traditionnel. Moscou, Pékin et plusieurs autres délégations veulent préserver le cadre onusien et empêcher toute modification unilatérale du mandat. D’autres membres soutiennent l’initiative marocaine d’autonomie, mais refusent que l’autodétermination soit écartée ou que l’issue des négociations soit prédéterminée. La conséquence immédiate est une situation d’impasse. L’expiration du mandat prive la MINURSO d’une nouvelle autorisation du Conseil pour poursuivre ses activités au-delà de cette échéance. Elle ne signifie toutefois pas que le Conseil de sécurité est dessaisi du dossier. Le paragraphe 6 de la résolution 2797 est explicite : le Conseil « décide de rester saisi de la question ». Cette disposition ne proroge pas le mandat de la MINURSO, mais confirme que le dossier du Sahara occidental demeure sous la responsabilité du Conseil. La fin du mandat de la mission ne vaut donc ni clôture du dossier onusien ni extinction de la compétence du Conseil. Avenir de la Minurso : trois scénarios possibles Cette distinction appelle une réponse à l’argument développé par le 360.ma pour réduire la portée du paragraphe 6 de la résolution 2797 au motif qu’il ne crée aucun mandat pour la MINURSO. C’est exact, mais hors sujet. Ce paragraphe confirme que le Conseil de sécurité demeure saisi du dossier et conserve sa compétence pour l’examiner et prendre de nouvelles décisions. L’expiration du mandat de la mission ne signifie donc ni dessaisissement du Conseil ni clôture du dossier onusien. La contradiction est d’autant plus manifeste que Rabat a présenté cette même résolution comme une consécration majeure de ses thèses, lui vouant un respect quasi sacré. La résolution ne saurait être intangible lorsqu’elle sert le Maroc et insignifiante lorsqu’elle contrarie son récit de victoire. Trois scénarios sont désormais possibles : une prorogation technique de la MINURSO, un compromis temporaire pour préserver la mission, ou le retour d’un texte américain remanié. À défaut d’accord, le mandat pourrait expirer, privant la mission de sa base juridique et ouvrant la voie à sa fermeture. L’article Conseil de sécurité : derrière le soutien au texte américain, de profondes réserves sur la position marocaine est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Babacar Cissé, un médaillé olympique dans l’ombre
items.description: Médaillé d’argent en judo aux premiers Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (Joj), en 2010 à Singapour, Babacar Cissé regrette de ne pas avoir été associé aux préparatifs de « Dakar 2026 ». Dans un entretien avec Tággat, l’ancien judoka est revenu sur les difficultés rencontrées lors de son parcours et plaide pour une meilleure reconnaissance des anciens champions, dont l’expérience pourrait servir d’exemple à la nouvelle génération. L’histoire du Sénégal avec les Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (Joj) n’a pas commencé en 2026. Babacar Cissé en est une illustration. Il fait partie des premiers Sénégalais à avoir participé à cette compétition. En 2010, à Singapour, le jeune judoka avait décroché une médaille d’argent dans l’épreuve par équipes mixtes. Âgé de 18 ans, il avait réalisé cette performance malgré des conditions de préparation difficiles. « Le seul hic, c’était le manque d’encadrement », confie-t-il. À l’époque, il avait quitté Dakar sans entraîneur et avec un kimono prêté. « On a dû me prêter un kimono au Sénégal pour que je puisse compétir », raconte-t-il. Sur place, il avait également bénéficié de l’aide d’un ressortissant togolais pour l’accompagner à la table officielle. « Ce n’est que lorsque je suis admis en finale que la délégation sénégalaise m’a rejoint », se souvient-il. Malgré ces difficultés, le judoka affirme avoir remporté tous ses combats individuels avant que son équipe ne s’incline en finale. « C’était quand même magnifique, ces Jeux, avec l’esprit de solidarité et de partage entre athlètes qui s’amusaient alors qu’ils n’étaient pas du même pays », retient-il de cette expérience. Dans un entretien accordé au média sportif Tággat, le 28 octobre, Babacar Cissé est également revenu sur son parcours et sa situation actuelle. Après plusieurs années passées sur les tatamis, il a arrêté la compétition en 2019, en raison notamment de ses activités professionnelles. Il travaille aujourd’hui comme postier à Mbour. L’ancien médaillé regrette de ne pas avoir été associé aux préparatifs des Joj « Dakar 2026 ». Il déplore également le manque de reconnaissance dont il estime avoir fait l’objet à son retour de Singapour avec sa médaille. « Je suis rentré avec une médaille de vice-champion olympique, et les autres ont été bien accueillis dans leurs pays », regrette-t-il. Pour lui, il est nécessaire de mieux accompagner les athlètes et de valoriser leurs performances. « C’est bien beau d’organiser des Jeux, mais il faudra décrocher des médailles. On n’organise pas pour perdre. Il faut renforcer l’encadrement des athlètes », estime Babacar Cissé. Marieme Fatou DRAMÉ

items.title: Journée des martyrs : Le Burkina Faso rend hommage aux victimes de l’insurrection et du putsch de 2015
items.description: Le Burkina Faso commémore, ce 31 octobre 2026, la Journée nationale des martyrs au Monument des Héros nationaux, à Ouagadougou. La cérémonie a été marquée par une minute de silence et un dépôt de gerbes en mémoire des victimes de l’insurrection populaire des 30 et 31 octobre 2014 et de la résistance au coup d’État manqué de septembre 2015, par le Président de l'Assemblée Législative du Peuple, Ousmane Bougouma. Douze ans après l’insurrection populaire qui a conduit à la chute du régime de Blaise Compaoré, les familles des victimes ont renouvelé leur appel à préserver la mémoire des martyrs et à poursuivre la quête de justice. Dans leur message, elles ont remercié les autorités pour le maintien de cette commémoration dans l’agenda national. Les familles appellent à poursuivre la lutte Dans leur déclaration, les familles des victimes ont rappelé que leurs proches sont tombés sous les balles les 30 et 31 octobre 2014, à Ouagadougou et dans d’autres localités du pays. Elles ont salué la continuité de la commémoration, qu’elles considèrent comme une reconnaissance du sacrifice des martyrs. Elles ont également exprimé leur soutien au Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, et appelé les Burkinabè, y compris ceux de la diaspora, à soutenir les actions du gouvernement et de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES). Leur message a aussi rendu hommage aux forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) ainsi qu’aux volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP) engagés dans la lutte contre l’insécurité. Oscibi Johann insiste sur le devoir de mémoire-©Faso7 Présent à la cérémonie, le reggaeman Oscibi Johann, à l’état civil Ouédraogo Sibiri Joanny, a insisté sur l’importance de préserver la mémoire des victimes. Blessé lors de la résistance au coup d’État de septembre 2015, l’artiste a salué la tenue de cette commémoration et remercié les autorités pour les efforts engagés en faveur des victimes. « Le peuple pardonne. Mais aujourd’hui nous n’oublions pas nos camarades. Ils sont tombés pour une cause. La cause, c’est la dignité. La cause, c’est que le Burkinabè doit croire en lui » , a-t-il déclaré. Pour l’artiste, les événements de 2014 et la résistance au putsch de 2015 ont marqué l’histoire politique du Burkina Faso. Il estime que les sacrifices consentis par les manifestants et les résistants doivent continuer à inspirer les générations actuelles, notamment dans la défense de la dignité et de la souveraineté nationale. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article Journée des martyrs : Le Burkina Faso rend hommage aux victimes de l’insurrection et du putsch de 2015 est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

Les directeurs des Infrastructures et du Désenclavement, Alioune Sène, et de la Mobilité et de la Circulation routière, Moustapha Niang, ont tenu à sensibiliser les conducteurs de motos-Jakarta durant le déroulement des Joj. Selon M. Sène, la réussite de cet événement ne dépendra pas uniquement de la qualité de l'organisation sportive, mais également de notre capacité collective à garantir la sécurité des personnes et la fluidité des déplacements. À cet égard, il a invité ces conducteurs de deux-roues évoluant dans les zones accueillant les compétitions à respecter cinq exigences : le respect strict du Code de la route et des limitations de vitesse ; le port systématique du casque de protection ; le respect des itinéraires et des dispositions spéciales de circulation mises en place pour les Joj ; la courtoisie et le respect des autres usagers de la route ; et, enfin, l'abandon des comportements dangereux. « Nous devons tous contribuer à assurer une circulation organisée, sécurisée et fluide », affirme-t-il, en les appelant à collaborer pleinement avec les Forces de défense et de sécurité. Le directeur des Infrastructures et du Désenclavement les exhorte également à être des « ambassadeurs de la sécurité routière » et de « l'hospitalité sénégalaise ». Afin de relever ce défi organisationnel et citoyen, plusieurs gilets et casques, dont 200 ont été distribués aux conducteurs de Diamniadio, ont été offerts à l'initiative de Mamadou Faye, dit « Lampe Fall », un agent du ministère des Transports terrestres et aériens. Au total, 1 000 casques ont été distribués, avec un ciblage des sites abritant les compétitions olympiques : 400 casques à Saly (Mbour) ; 200 casques pour le site d'Iba Mar Diop ; 200 casques pour le site de Diamniadio. En dehors de ce triangle, 200 casques ont été distribués à Louga. Pour le directeur de la Mobilité et de la Circulation routière, Moustapha Niang, le port du casque constitue une mesure essentielle de protection et devrait devenir un réflexe indispensable. « Le casque n'est pas un accessoire, c'est un équipement qui sauve des vies », soutient-il. Ce message est partagé par le président des conducteurs de motos-Jakarta, qui lance le slogan : « Mon casque, ma sécurité sur la route ». Selon eux, conduire sans porter de casque comporte plusieurs risques. Ils s'engagent à mener un plaidoyer auprès des leurs pour renforcer davantage la sécurité routière. Mohamed DIENE (Correspondant)

items.title: What the Economy Is Sacrificing to AI
items.description: Over the past four years, Dallas, the beating heart of the U.S. energy economy, has become the beating heart of the U.S. data-center economy. That’s thanks to its cheap land, friendly regulatory posture, liquid labor market, excellent transportation infrastructure, and ample grid connectivity. Roughly 125 facilities are up and running in the metro region, and an additional 19 are under construction and 53 are planned. The building boom is boosting wages for blue-collar workers and helping hold the local unemployment rate at 4.1 percent, close to its historic low. Yet Dallas and its suburbs are also in the midst of a building bust. Retail construction is strong. But despite high rents and a growing population, few new homes are being built: The number of houses builders broke ground on dropped 12 percent year-over-year, and the number of multifamily units in the works plummeted 43 percent over the past three years . Office construction is also depressed. Is the tech boom offsetting these other downturns or causing them? That’s the big question facing Dallas and the rest of the United States. Investors are more pumped about AI than they have been about any technology since the railroad . If they weren’t directing a torrent of money to the handful of firms finessing algorithms and constructing data centers, the country’s employment level and economic output might be lower. Then again, if they weren’t directing a torrent of money to the handful of firms finessing algorithms and constructing data centers, they might be directing it to everyone and everything else. So is AI fueling the American economy or siphoning gas from it? Is it “crowding out” investment in non-tech enterprises, as economists put it, or boosting investment in an otherwise lackluster expansion? [ Rogé Karma: Something ominous is happening in the AI economy ] Certainly, AI is pushing up GDP—or, to be precise, the AI build-out is pushing up GDP. In 2020, American businesses spent $3.6 trillion, adjusting for inflation, on investments in durable assets, such as software, warehouses, and trucks. Last year, they spent $4.4 trillion. Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Alphabet are shelling out $800 billion on capital expenditures just this year , a sum that has grown eightfold over the decade. It’s a Silicon Valley hard-hat stimulus, bigger than the one Washington passed to counter the Great Recession. And it is transforming national accounts. In this year’s second quarte r , household consumption rose at a 3.8 percent annualized pace. Private investment in everything but real estate climbed at a pace of 12.7 percent. Spending on equipment went up at a 21 percent rate. Purchases of computers alone added 0.7 percentage points to GDP, and “information processing equipment” a mammoth 0.9 percentage points. This private-sector stimulus has as much to do with New York, London, and Shanghai as it does with Cupertino and San Francisco. The early AI boom was mostly financed by wildly wealthy venture capitalists and wildly profitable tech companies, many of the investors staking cash. But soon, AI firms needed more computing power to perfect their models. They needed to build data centers and chip factories. They needed hundreds of billions of dollars more liquidity than the Bay Area could provide. The world’s investors took a look at the sparkling returns they were promising and signed on. The cost of loans climbed as demand for loans climbed. Crowd out crowded in. The effect is easiest to see in the construction sector. AI-linked firms are currently building 543 data centers, and 2,513 more are in the pipeline. Spending on the build-out has increased 65 percent over the past year, according to an analysis by the Harvard economist Jason Furman. At the same time, the amount devoted to building housing and retail outlets has dropped 10 percent. Spending on the construction of education facilities is down 13 percent; offices, 14 percent; hotels, motels, and resorts, 15 percent; and manufacturing plants, 24 percent. Tech enterprises are not merely making it more expensive for non-tech enterprises to finance construction projects. They’re bidding up the cost of labor, land, and materials. They’re spurring landlords and institutional investors to buy Treasuries or stocks instead of bothering with apartment buildings and retirement homes. They’re forcing families to pay more for home loans too. As a general point, high yields are “sucking all the money out of the mortgage market,” Daryl Fairweather, the chief economist at Redfin, told me. Governments trying to build infrastructure are getting hit by the same increase in borrowing costs. So are families looking to buy a new car or renovate a property. So are young people looking to launch a small business or sign up for a training program. In a roundabout way, Claude and ChatGPT might be increasing credit-card delinquencies as well. Granted, the effect might not be that big outside of the construction and real-estate sectors, which are highly sensitive to interest rates and overhead expenses. (The trade war, immigration crackdown, and war with Iran are pummeling them too.) Justin Wolfers, an economist at the University of Michigan, noted that “2007 through 2022 was an unusual period” in which borrowing costs were close to zero. Today, rates have returned to where they were in the 1990s, and they remain lower than they were in the 1980s. They are “what I would call normal,” he said. Moreover, higher interest rates force investors to think before they stake, squeezing out the frothiest, goofiest, and scammiest projects first. Cryptocurrency mining facilities are “clearly being crowded out,” Ryan Cummings, an economist at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, told me. He called that “a good thing.” [ Andy Masley: The data-center debate is divorced from the facts ] Then again, houses and apartment buildings are a good thing, as are factories and hotels. Small, AI-driven changes in interest rates might lead to hundreds of thousands of American families remaining renters for the next decade. They might lead to scores of commercial outlets not getting built. They might lead to hundreds of non-tech start-ups remaining nothing more than an idea. Will all of these data centers be a good thing, aside from their utility to AI firms? Perhaps not. Normally, cities and towns become more prosperous and credit-worthy when they lure companies to build facilities there. “It’s a two-plus-two-equals-five argument,” Jess Cornaggia, a finance professor at Pennsylvania State University, told me. Power plants, schools, stadiums, and factories hire workers, generate revenue for local businesses, increase tax receipts, and spur additional firms to co-locate. But data centers might end up being a two-plus-two-equals-four, or even two-plus-two-equals-three, proposition. Investors are demanding larger yields on bonds for water and school projects in communities with a lot of data centers, meaning they expect those communities to experience more resource strains and collect less property-tax revenue in the future. Once data centers are up and running, they use a considerable amount of power and water while generating close to no jobs, after all. These trade-offs have been mostly absent from the hyped-up debate over AI’s effect on welfare and wealth, but they’re important. Giving up homes, parks, health clinics, and grocery stores might be worth it if white-collar firms become radically more productive and creative. Giving up non-tech start-ups might be worth it if we get a cure for cancer. But the more resources the country devotes to AI at the expense of other innovations, the more its future depends on that bet paying off.

items.title: The Bursting of the Tel Aviv Bubble
items.description: N o one talks about the left in Israel anymore. The label itself is essentially a curse word, something spat out by an angry taxi driver after he’s swerved around a guy on a scooter. A measly 12 to 15 percent of Israelis identify as such. But democracy has a much better reputation, at least in cosmopolitan, beachy Tel Aviv, which is maybe why the leftmost party running for parliament in this week’s election gave itself the name the Democrats. A liberal ethos lives here, alongside excellent coffee, delicious salads, and fashion boutiques. The city has been the epicenter of protest against Benjamin Netanyahu’s government over the past four years. Itamar Ben-Gvir, Netanyahu’s far-right interior minister, has taken to calling it “the state of Tel Aviv,” and its population of tech workers, baristas, and academics “anarchists”—enemies whose openness threatens the purer Jewish state he dreams about. The state of Tel Aviv, not exactly an inaccurate sobriquet, girded itself for the election this week and then got battered. The results can’t be called anything other than inconclusive. Cobbling together a new governing coalition, for either Netanyahu or his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, looks near-impossible. But Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc got 53 seats to the 48 for Eisenkot’s “change” bloc, and this was far from the win much of Tel Aviv expected and badly needed. I’ve heard the same refrain over and over this week. How could voters possibly elect Netanyahu again? After October 7. After the abandonment of the hostages. After the corruption. After his naked pursuit of power at all costs. The lies. The racism. And, in the days before the election, the proud embrace of the country’s increasing isolation. The world economy wants to boycott us? Fine , he said. We’ll shift to crypto . After all that. But there is also all the energy the city has put into rejecting Bibism (a shorthand as useful and yet nondescript as Trumpism ). Starting with the protests against the proposed changes to the judicial system after Netanyahu took power in 2022 and then the struggle to free the hostages in Gaza, Tel Avivians are so accustomed to protest that most have a kit ready with all they need (flag, water bottle, running shoes) for the Saturday-night gatherings that have become a ritual. Many of them are exhausted, and they expected this election to be a vindication. [ Read: Israel’s latest last chance to save itself ] I’ve spent the past week in Israel, speaking with people in Tel Aviv. The shock they are experiencing is twofold. First is the confirmation of their minority status in the country. Despite being the center of Israel’s economy and its cultural life, Tel Aviv seems even more isolated after this election, even more an exception, more set apart in its values and dreams—and getting ever smaller. “This is a blow, and it will be hard to pick up from this point and understand what the next steps are,” Oded Leshem, a political psychologist at Hebrew University and the author of Hope Amidst Conflict , told me. Others spoke of a moral disappointment in the country. “It should have been a landslide,” one distraught tattooed waiter said at a wine bar near Rabin Square. But another realization is quickly dawning. Perhaps the biggest story of the election was the success of the Arab parties. They managed to win 19 seats by bringing out voters in numbers never seen before. I experienced the enthusiasm personally the day before the election, standing on the outskirts of Abu Ghosh, an Arab Israeli village near Jerusalem, as people commuted to work. I was with canvassers trying to get out the vote, and for two hours, women in hijabs and large sunglasses and men in pickup trucks rolled down their windows to yell out that everyone they knew was going to vote—their brothers, mothers, grandfathers—and that something had to change. The village ended up having a 78 percent turnout, up from 55 percent in 2022. The anti-Arab policies of Netanyahu’s government had triggered a backlash. One Arab Israeli man in Jaffa told me that a Palestinian friend in the West Bank from Jenin, a man who can’t vote, had called him to make sure he cast a ballot, if only to help stop the settler violence. Every other election had only elicited cynicism from his Palestinian friends. Looking at the numbers, Eisenkot does have a path to leading a government, but only if he includes the Arab parties in his coalition. Their 19 seats and his 48 add up to a robust 67. This will not be an easy marriage, because most of the Jewish parties in his bloc have vowed to never join a government with Arab parties. This resistance is not based in racism, or not only in racism: Some of the Arab parties are openly anti-Zionist; they include a Palestinian right of return in their platforms; and even the most acceptable and pragmatic of Arab Israeli leaders, Mansour Abbas of Ra’am, is unwilling to explicitly renounce Hamas as a terrorist organization. That said, I’ve seen commentator after commentator laugh at the idea that the preelection vows of any political party, Jewish or Arab, are rock-solid—Netanyahu, the grand strategist, it’s often pointed out, once flirted with the idea of adding Ra’am to his coalition. The bigger shift will be a mental one. Israelis who want a liberal democracy can no longer afford to sideline the Arab parties. That was the message Arab Israeli communities sent: If liberal Tel Aviv has any hope of bringing its values to bear on the future of the country, it’s going to need those voters in Abu Ghosh. It’s going to need to see their significant inclusion as part of the democracy they are fighting for, even if this also means reopening arguments about the nature of the Jewish state, Palestinian rights, and the occupation. “You can’t be liberal and deny the Arab Israeli voters,” the screenwriter Avner Bernheimer told me. His film Yossi and Jagger was a breakthrough in the depiction of gay life in Israel, and he has been one of the leaders of the country’s LGBTQ movement. “Most of them feel a part of Israel. They are Israelis. They work; they are doctors and engineers and architects and business owners. We have to accept the fact that they are not our enemy. They want to be a part of the Israeli project. If liberals keep boycotting them, we will lose to the extreme religious right, the most violent groups, and the cult of Netanyahu.” T he next few weeks will determine the shape of Israel’s government. But what may not change is the sense of alienation within the Tel Aviv bubble, the feeling among these Israelis that they might not have a home here anymore. The stakes are not small. Putting the state of democracy and the worsening situation in the West Bank aside, Israel’s economy largely depends on this demographic. As much as 93 percent of all income-tax revenue comes from just 20 percent of Israel’s workers. And many are already leaving. From 2022 to 2024, according to a government report, Israel experienced a net loss of 140,000 citizens. If highly educated people leave—if they can’t see a future for themselves in a country where they are supporting a mostly unemployed ultra-Orthodox population and sending their children to the army when these religious families are not—then Israel may be headed the way of an impoverished theocracy, forever at war (a “Jewish Iran” is how one commenter put it on election night). My cousin Gideon, who fits the profile of Tel Aviv’s professional class (he’s a tech executive who likes good wine), put it bluntly to me: “If Bibi is elected, I’m not sure I’m going to stay here. And it’s enough that 100,000 people like me are leaving, and this country is toast.” The question of staying or going was particularly acute this week in Tel Aviv because about 70,000 Israelis who live abroad had come back to vote. People bumped into friends from Brooklyn or Berlin on Dizengoff Street. On the Sunday before the election, I went to a storytelling evening called Moadon Ktav—think Moth Radio Hour . It’s a regular event where creative types compete with one another in delivering seven-minute monologues responding to a pair of word prompts. For this particular evening, which drew an audience of 400 young hipsters, the chosen monologuists were Israelis who live abroad, and the chosen words— original versus translation , connect versus disengage —seemed designed to elicit their most emotional feelings about exile. The host, who wore aviator glasses and a gold chain, began the evening by asking the audience, “Why so stressed? What’s on the line? Only a country.” Heartbreak was a consistent theme: being caught between two existences, not fully comfortable anywhere. One woman living in Germany lamented that she would never be able to help her daughter with her homework. Another talked about leaving Israel to save his young son from being drafted in the future, only to realize that his child would now be a foreigner to him. [ Read: Fighting Israel to the last Palestinian ] Liad Mudrik, a professor of neuroscience and psychology at Tel Aviv University, was part of a group of researchers who saw an opportunity in the influx of expat Israeli academics arriving to “save the country,” as she put it. They suggested a mega-conference to take place just before the election, Mind IL—59 simultaneous conferences in different fields, including physics, philosophy, and art, with 5,500 participants, including 2,000 academics living abroad. Mudrik told me that many of these Israelis shared a common experience of feeling both ostracized abroad and ill at ease in Israel. She’s seen colleagues extend a sabbatical year or actively choose to look for work elsewhere. “What worries me is that if Israel doesn’t change its course, many more academics and professionals will decide to leave the country,” she said. “It would have a huge effect on Israel.” The ones who came back to vote did so because they could never not be Israeli, for better or worse. “I’ve been the Iron Dome of Israel in San Francisco over the past three years,” Hadar Aviram, a law professor at the UC Law San Francisco told me. Students had dropped her classes, and the animal-rights organization where she was doing pro bono work stopped using her as a lawyer. She had no ethical qualms about voting even though she no longer lived in Israel. “My conscience is clear.” T he intellectual who perhaps most symbolized this liberal, democratic Israel—who could be deemed the creator of its source text, in a way—was Amos Oz, the novelist, who died in 2018. He expressed the self-effacing values of the kibbutz, took a consistent moral stand against the occupation after 1967, and deeply loved and exalted the secular Hebrew culture that took shape in the cafés of Tel Aviv. His daughter Fania Oz-Salzberger, a historian, continues to promote these ideas, including the necessity of full Arab participation in Israeli political life. That her main method of communication is posting on X, where she regularly tangles with trolls, says something about today’s world. I met Oz-Salzberger, who has her father’s crystal-blue eyes, at a café on Allenby Street the day before the election. She was nervous. Even a “dead heat,” she said, would indicate “a terrible failure,” because, as she saw it, “the liberal-democratic muscle is being pushed to the max.” She expressed worries I’d been hearing in many of my conversations—about violence, about the degradation of the country over the past four years, about whether her two sons, both studying at Oxford, would choose to come back. But her response was also more combative than I expected. Oz-Salzberger was done with compromises with the Orthodox and extreme-right parts of Israeli society. After decades of taking part in cross-cultural conversations—including those her father started—she no longer wanted to make nice, she said. “We’re saying to the settlers, we’re saying to the ultra-Orthodox: ‘We’ve played the game long enough. And there is no longer a common denominator between us.’” She told me she had even contemplated the need for a militia to counter the armed settlers on the right. To hear this from the daughter of Amos Oz, in defense of the “humanist Zionism” she still believes is possible, made clear just how much she feels she has already lost. Yishai Sarid, a lawyer and novelist, offered even darker prognostications. Sarid is another scion of what he calls “good old Israel”; his father was Yossi Sarid, a leading figure of the left. “I’ve lived with a feeling of being in a minority since a very young age,” Yishai told me. In 1974, when Yishai was 9, his father, newly elected to the Knesset, moved the family to the northern border town of Kiryat Shmona and began teaching civics at the local high school. He wanted to express solidarity with the town, where 18 people had just been killed in a terrorist attack, and also to try to “heal the rifts” between the center and the periphery by moving his family to a place where Tel Aviv elites of his sort don’t usually live. (Hezbollah still regularly attacks the town with missiles, but its population just voted for Netanyahu by nearly 50 percent, an astounding figure given how much it has suffered under him.) The time in Kiryat Shmona was lonely and difficult for Yishai. His father’s politics—especially his early and definite stance on the necessity of making peace with the Palestinians—always made him feel marginal. The big turning point in Yishai Sarid’s life came in 1995, when Prime Minister Yitzchak Rabin was assassinated shortly after negotiating the Oslo Accords. He understood right away that the country would never be the same. For years, he could not bear to walk by what is now known as Rabin Square, where the prime minister was killed. Many of the novels he’s written since explore the darkness that was let loose that day and has come to dominate Israel, as he sees it. The Third Temple , published in 2015, imagines that the dreams of the religious fanatics have been fulfilled and the Jewish temple in Jerusalem has been restored, along with ritual sacrifice. He laughed when his agent told him that it had been nominated for a science-fiction award. I asked Sarid whether he thought the country’s religious extremists actually wanted to bring back sacrifice. “Of course they do,” he said. “They’re training for it.” In Jerusalem, he said, religious groups have taken to wearing ancient priestly garments and every Passover rehearsing the ritual slaughter of sheep. He has no doubt that this is where Israel is headed. “The temple,” he said. “Everything leads there.” F undamentalism and sectarianism have become the baseline in Israeli society for the past three decades, the reality that the liberal democrats of Israel find themselves pushing back against. The only way to change this dynamic, Itamar Weizman told me, is to change the culture of the left from one of reaction to something “fun, cool, and sexy.” Answer the temple, in other words, with the allure of the Tel Aviv beach. Weizman is a political activist wunderkind who, at only 34, has had a few careers already—in politics working for various politicians on the left, including Ehud Barak; in business as a venture capitalist and with a start-up focused on climate tech. Five years ago he started a nonprofit called Beit Radical (“Radical House”), a book publisher and an all-purpose community center in an abandoned fish market in an industrial section of south Tel Aviv. The design is brutalist chic: lots of concrete and native plants. There’s a café outside and a nightclub in the basement. A rooftop garden is in the works. Weizman sees his role as making engagement in Israeli society attractive for those who would leave. “I want them not to go to Berlin,” he said. “I want Berlin to come to them.” Weizman showed me around Beit Radical before the election. He moved and talked quickly, emptying ashtrays and picking up dirty coffee cups as we went along. Back in 2015, when he was 21, Weizmen headed a grassroots initiative called V15, through which he attempted to bring community organizing to Israel. Netanyahu tried to ban the group because it was funded in part by foreign nonprofits. Weizman said he shifted his focus to culture. The center hosts multiple events and activities every week, including lectures and concerts. “I missed the future,” Weizman said. What brings young people to the center—multiple teenagers and 20-somethings told me that Beit Radical was their place—is a desire to feel confident again, to not always be reacting to the right, to begin to think ahead. And, crucially, to smile while doing it. This all sounded great, but I was struck by how homogeneous the young people hanging out at the café smoking cigarettes seemed, and I wondered out loud how Weizman planned to expand beyond the circle of upper-middle-class Ashkenazi Jews who frequent the center. He told me about plans to open up new Beit Radicals in places such as Haifa, which has a large Arab population, and Beer Sheva, a poorer town in the south. This seems a step beyond the bubble, which, given Israel’s demographics, will be necessary if Weizman hopes to move these young people past talking to themselves. Vered Adir Mili Eshet and Or Schraiber in Asaph Polonsky’s forthcoming film, In Person. I chose to watch the election returns at Beit Radical, and, as Weizman promised, the night was indeed joyous—until 10 o’clock. The center’s courtyard was full: A crowd of about 2,000 was loudly singing, jumping up and down, under a glowing sign with a lyric from an old peace anthem, “Bring on the Day.” Rami Fortis, a Billy Idol–ish punk rocker famous since the 1970s, now 72, bald, and wearing glasses, was growling from the stage. But at 10 o’clock, the election-night broadcast was projected on a stuccoed wall of a neighboring building, and it was as if someone had pressed a mute button on the party. Unlike in American elections, with their slow drip of state-by-state results, in Israel, exit polls projecting how the votes have been apportioned to the various parties are released all at once. These numbers can turn out to be wrong, but they provide a rough immediate snapshot and begin a battle over the narrative. The first piece of information was that Netanyahu’s Likud party was projected to win 25 seats, which would give him the most votes in the next Parliament (the final number would be 27); no one quite seemed to notice just then how well the Arab parties had done. Within five minutes, the courtyard cleared out. People made for the exit with their heads bowed or glancing back painfully at the screen. In no time at all—only enough to take a few breaths—cautious hope had disintegrated into disappointment. “It can’t be. It can’t be,” one woman with a pixie haircut was crying into her phone. A shaggy-haired young guy with a mustache, a stranger, put his hand on her shoulder and said quietly, “It happened.” M any of the Arab Israelis I spoke with expressed pride in the numbers that came out to vote. And in the current limbo a few days past the vote, as backroom deals are being struck between various parties, they are waiting to see what happens, maybe more than any other demographic in Israel. The 19 seats the Arab parties won has forced a question that the mainstream Israeli political establishment has sought to ignore: How serious is it about Arab integration and shared political power? It’s one thing to point with pride at Israeli democracy (“the only democracy in the Middle East,” detractors are often reminded); it’s another thing to actually hand out ministerial portfolios to Arab citizens. The Arabs I talked with said they have always felt a little gaslit by this democracy talk. Now comes a moment of truth. This wasn’t entirely expected, and the change bloc still seems to be reeling from the understanding that its only path to power will be doing something dramatic and brave on this particular front. The fight it expected, and the issue largely responsible for getting more people involved in the liberal-democratic cause, was over the conscription of ultra-Orthodox men into the army. Polling data show that 72 percent of Israelis support the idea. (The Arab parties also oppose mandatory conscription to the army, but some, like Ra’am, are open to the idea of a national service program.) The debate over this matter always points back to citizenship, to what an individual owes to society. Now a different but related citizenship question is going to dominate: What does a society owe to its citizens? [ Graeme Wood: Israel can’t postpone its reckoning forever ] The language for talking about Arab Israeli citizenship is already there. You could hear it in the way that Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former police commissioner, explained his decision to join Ra’am. In an X post, he conjured the image of a hospital. “There, one sheds narratives and identities; there, first and foremost, people meet. Patients, doctors, nurses, administrative staff, families—everyone is equal. That is the place where we are all human beings, and that is where we will begin.” Segalovich is trying to normalize the sharing of political power with Arabs, to bring them into full partnership as citizens, something Israel’s Declaration of Independence demands. In the hours after the results showed a significant majority for the change bloc plus the Arab parties—in other words, a 67–53 majority for ousting Netanyahu—Segalovich declared victory, countering the glumness. “My intention is to break the lines between Arabs and Jews,” he said in an interview just after the results were reported. Whether the politicians he hopes to share a coalition with feel likewise, and whether Eisenkot is capable of making the case for Arab inclusion, may not depend on idealism— a desire for coexistence, or an appreciation of Arab citizenship. It may demand that Israeli Jews to set aside some of their most deeply held convictions about the Jewish character of the state in favor of realpolitik. Simply put, if Eisenkot and his partners want to lead Israel and oust Netanyahu, then for their own sake, they must join with the Arabs. I heard this self-interested approach in something that Raef Zreik, the Arab Israeli jurist and scholar, told me in the days before the election. He was generally skeptical that the results would change the lives of Palestinians in Israel or the West Bank, but he did see the possibility of improvement by focusing on pragmatism. Only a priest can look into the inner state of mind of a political actor, he told me. As a Palestinian, he was not going to wait for the hearts of Jewish Israelis to change. More important was whether they could be convinced that change served their own interests. “Sometimes it doesn’t matter what you think; what matters more is the way you act,” Zreik said. If you’re a member of the Ashkenazi Tel Aviv elite and pursuing your own interests, you might feel threatened by extreme-right forces in your own society, he said, and “in order to save yourself, as a side effect, you might want to enlarge the space for liberal individual democratic freedoms along the way.” At least some Israeli Jews are seeing this as an opportunity. President Isaac Herzog will soon have the task of deciding whom to appoint to form a new government: the candidate whose party got the most votes (Netanyahu) or the one who has the greatest potential of forming a coalition (arguably Eisenkot, if he includes the Arab parties). A long list of prominent Israeli legal scholars, former judges, academics, and public intellectuals have signed a petition asking that the president consider what Israel’s Arab citizens have expressed through their vote: a desire to play a full and equal role in the political process. Affirming this desire, they write, could be essential “to the future of democracy and the fabric of Israeli society.” O n election day, I wandered the shady boulevards of Tel Aviv, past the kiosks selling espressos and fresh juice. Occasionally, I would check in on Asaph Polonsky, a filmmaker whose movies have been in competition in Cannes. He lives in Los Angeles and had come to Israel to vote, but also to make a feature film called In Person . [ Graeme Wood: Israeli election results hazy, try again ] The concept reminded me of Before Sunrise , the Richard Linklater movie. In Polonsky’s story, Mili and Or, two Israelis, are exes who no longer live in Israel but have returned to vote. They run into each other on the street and begin a conversation that will last throughout the day as they walk the city and end up in Jaffa, where they will watch the election returns together. Polonsky was filming in Dizengoff Square, at the center of the city’s shopping district, when I caught up with him. The giant fountain there is ringed by photos of hostages and memorials to dead soldiers. Photos of these young people also dangle from the branches of trees bordering the square. Mili and Or sat on a bench arguing. She was worried about raising a child in Israel and was glad to be gone. He has a child and told her that parenting is a worrisome business wherever you are. Polonsky stood behind the camera’s monitor with headphones on. Around him swirled the chaos of Tel Aviv, which seems so vibrant that it’s hard to imagine it ever ending—groups of teenagers taking selfies, canvassers dressed all in pink and yelling at people through megaphones to go vote, strangers petting one another’s dogs. Polonsky told me that all of this noise would be part of the film and that it was only roughly scripted. How it concluded would depend largely on what actually happened with the vote. He didn’t want to give too much away, understandably, and wasn’t looking for easy analogies, but it wasn’t hard to picture a will-they-won’t-they storyline being as much about this couple as about the relationship with a country. Polonsky said he had been hoping for the sake of his plot that the change bloc would win. “It would make for a happy ending,” he said. But instead something much harder to film happened: a continuation of unresolved tension, deadlock. Maybe this was good for the story, Polonsky said. The film was ultimately about what can be changed and what cannot be changed. Could these old lovers rekindle a flame, or had too much happened? At that moment in Jaffa, though, the cameras trained on Mila’s and Or’s faces as they watched the news revealed no ambiguity, at least as Polonsky saw it. “Their eyes looked the way you do when you don’t get what you want,” he said. “Which happens a lot.”

items.title: Trump Has Pushed Some Texas Republicans Too Far
items.description: T he tiny Yorkshire terrier in a diaper was not central to my experience in Tarrant County, but she did set the tone. Tia was the first creature to greet me when I arrived at Hillary Shepheard’s townhouse in Texas last week. She yapped until I settled into a chair at the kitchen island, when she switched to a minuscule growl. “Sorry,” Shepheard told me. “She always does this.” Shepheard, the blond-haired, 34-year-old leader of the Tarrant County Young Republicans, would apologize a dozen more times during the next half hour: for the clutter, for having forgotten to put on her “face” before I arrived, for leaving the charcuterie board to the very last minute. “My mom would kill me if she knew,” Shepheard said, plopping grapes into a colander. Her voice sounded raspy. She’d just gotten over the flu. Life is chaotic for any political operative two weeks ahead of an important election. But the midterms have taxed Shepheard emotionally, too. In fact, this was the reason for our charcuterie gathering, which involved three other Tarrant County Republicans: a former politician, a party activist, and a professor. The five of us spent the evening discussing the midterms, which for some Texas conservatives pose a moral test that is bigger even than Donald Trump: whether or not to vote for Ken Paxton. I have had several memorable experiences in Texas over the past year. In Lubbock, I was escorted from a Jasmine Crockett rally by armed guards. In Allen, I watched Paxton fans consume countless margaritas in celebration of President Trump’s long-awaited endorsement. And in Tyler, I saw Democrats gaze at James Talarico like an oasis in the desert. [ Read: ‘Elaine from Atlantic … she needs to leave’ ] But nothing has been quite as instructive as listening to a group of Texas conservatives decide, in real time, how best to meet this current political moment. The choice seems anything but straightforward; they’ve been asked to fall in line behind a Senate nominee with enough baggage to fill a container ship. What happens on Tuesday will hinge on the decisions of people like the ones in Shepheard’s living room. After much internal debate, Tia’s owner had made her own choice clear. For the long-term survival of her party, she told us, “Ken Paxton has to lose.” T he five of us sat in white chairs around a glass table in Shepheard’s living room, stacking cheddar cubes on crackers from her hastily made spread. But our conversation didn’t begin with Paxton. It began, as so much seems to, with Trump. All but one of the conservatives in the room said they’d voted for him all three times, although none seemed the type to put on a red baseball cap and do the YMCA. Shepheard had assembled a group of highly engaged, deeply partisan Texans, diverse in style if not ideology. “When you describe me, Brad Pitt–esque is totally fine,” John Huffman, a 43-year-old entrepreneur and the former mayor of Southlake, told me (although his beard actually makes him look more like Oscar Isaac in Dune ). Huffman’s attitude toward Trump has always been conflicted—but it seemed representative in the group. A self-described “Christian conservative,” he has never supported Trump in a primary election, but ultimately voted for him every time in November. He was disturbed by the events of January 6, but believed that Trump’s second administration “had an incredible amount of promise.” He’d hoped that the president would improve the economy, deport only violent “illegals,” and implement a more coherent tariff strategy. But now? Huffman feels that Trump has done the opposite on virtually all counts and started a brand-new war. It “makes no sense,” he said, as Shepheard nodded along. The president built a powerful coalition, “and less than two years later, he squandered it.” Jill Tate, a 53-year-old Republican activist and the president of the Texas Federation of Republican Women, hadn’t been a Trump primary voter either. But she offered a softer assessment of his second term. “ Most things I’ve been happy with,” she told the group. “There are certain things that I think make him …” Tate trailed off, sighed, and looked into the distance. She was trying to choose her words carefully. “He’s brought a different element to the party,” she went on after a moment. “He’s not a Reagan Republican; he’s his own brand of Republican, and that is one of the reasons the party’s looking differently.” With what was perhaps the understatement of the century, we had reached the crux of our conversation. Trump has remade the Texas Republican Party in his image, transforming it into a machine built not for winning general elections, but for allowing him to dominate poisonous primaries. “What we have,” Huffman said, “is a fractured set of relationships that we are finding harder and harder to mend.” This reconfiguration has facilitated the rise of questionable characters and reactionaries. Bo French, the former chair of the Tarrant County Republican Party, once shared a poll asking whether Jews or Muslims were a bigger threat to America. Now French is the billionaire-backed Republican nominee for railroad commissioner, a job overseeing gas and oil in Texas. He continues to post bigoted messages . Then there is Paxton. The three-term Texas attorney general is well known by now for facing accusations of securities fraud and bribery, for his alleged extramarital affairs, and for his less important but notable decision to pocket a $1,000 pen that did not belong to him. Still, many Texas Republicans adore Paxton for his commitment to MAGA. Others support Paxton in spite of the fact that his name appears to evoke instant and obvious disgust. At a “Come and Take It” rally for Paxton last week, one man told me he’d vote for the attorney general, even as he made a face. In another ringing endorsement, an elderly woman said she’d “vote for the devil himself” before siding with Paxton’s opponent. Two Republicans in our group seemed to share this sentiment, even if they wouldn’t put it quite that way. Brandon Chicotsky, a 41-year-old marketing professor at Texas Christian University and the faculty adviser for its Turning Point chapter, was the only one who did not vote for Trump in 2016; he’d supported the Libertarian candidate, Gary Johnson. Sitting across from me at Shepheard’s house, he explained that the charges against Paxton and French were not enough to dissuade him. “I don’t like these people,” he said, “but I find it imperative for the function of government that they win.” Straightforward. So was Tate: “While you may have issues with Paxton, he’s gonna vote Republican,” she said, looking around at the others. Even after ugly primaries, Texas Republicans can usually be relied upon to fall in line come November. (See: Trump’s victories in 2016 and 2024.) But Huffman and Shepheard said they just weren’t willing to do it this time. Neither plans to vote for Paxton or French. “Our party needs a slap in the face,” Shepheard said. The pair, she added later in a follow-up call, can’t “define the Republican Party to the outside world.” Huffman agreed. “I held my nose and voted for Trump three times, knowing that he didn’t share a lot of my moral compass,” but voting for Paxton “would be admitting to myself and my family and my friends that character truly doesn’t matter as long as your jersey is Republican.” I admitted to being a little confused. Paxton and Trump have a remarkably similar set of ethical problems. Why support one but draw a line at the other? It was a question Huffman said he’d thought a lot about. The presidency matters more than a single Senate seat, he answered. “There’s also part of me that understands the compromise I had to make to vote for Trump, and maybe this is my way of reclaiming a little bit of that.” Tate, a Republican activist for more than three decades, seemed to be struggling. She nodded occasionally as Huffman talked, but she was frustrated to hear him say this. The Texas legislature is red. The governor is a Republican. “We are exactly where we wanted to be 30 years ago,” she said. The Democrats stopped winning in Texas because the party couldn’t stay united, she added. “If we lose one statewide, the door is open. We cannot let it be open.” But Huffman and Shepheard believe it’s too late—that Trump and his allies ripped the door off its hinges years ago. Last year, in a special election to fill a vacancy in the state Senate, Huffman lost a bitter three-way fight to a self-described “ultra-MAGA” candidate and a Democrat. The district, which Trump had won by 17 points in 2024, elected the Democrat by 14. (The “ultra-MAGA” candidate is running again this year but has since shed the label.) If Paxton loses, perhaps Texas Republicans will feel compelled to reform the way the party runs primaries—which might, in turn, allow more reasonable, less morally compromised candidates to be successful. “Ken Paxton losing,” Huffman said, “may be the thing that could save the Republican Party in Texas.” S o, will the Paxton naysayers be voting for James Talarico? As if. “I’m perfectly comfortable leaving that particular race blank,” Shepheard told me, although she would vote for Jon Rosenthal, the Democrat and former oil-field engineer running against French. “Talarico is a heretic, and a hard-left progressive,” Huffman said, not an unusual take among conservative Christians, who have been startled to hear Talarico defend abortion on biblical grounds and argue that God is nonbinary. [ Read: Things are about to get ugly in Texas ] Talarico has made overtures to Republicans by appealing to faith and talking a lot about economic populism. In some cases, it’s worked: A parade of local and state GOP officials has publicly switched sides to support him. But most hard-core partisans, including the ones at Shepheard’s house, aren’t going to skip to the polls to cast a ballot for a Democrat. The ones who can stomach it will support Paxton. The ones who can’t will sit out the race altogether. Right now, polls show a tight Senate race, although Talarico has a slight, consistent edge. If the Democrat does defy the odds to win in November, his bipartisan appeal will be only a sliver of the story. A better explanation will be that Trump and his Republican allies in Texas have finally pushed their own voters too far.
